article.title: How to Install Cabinet Handles and Knobs (With a Jig)
article.summary: Install cabinet pulls and knobs that line up perfectly: pick the placement, set a drilling jig once, drill clean holes and tighten the hardware.
article.body:
New pulls and knobs are one of the fastest ways to update a kitchen. The hard part is getting dozens of holes in exactly the same spot. A drilling jig solves that. This guide covers new holes in unpainted, painted or stained wood and MDF cabinets.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: wear safety glasses when drilling. Remove drawers or clamp doors so they don't swing while you drill.

Steps

  1. Choose the hardware size and placement

    Pulls are sold by center-to-center distance between their screws, such as 3 in, 96 mm or 128 mm. A common rule is a pull about one-third the drawer width. On doors, place pulls or knobs on the stile (the frame side opposite the hinges), about 2 to 3 in from the top corner on base cabinets and from the bottom corner on wall cabinets. On drawers, center the pull.

    Done right: you've written one placement rule for doors and one for drawers, and you'll use it everywhere.

  2. Set the jig

    Set the cabinet hardware jig to your hardware's center-to-center spacing and your chosen distances from the edges. Lock every adjustment. Mark the first hole positions on one door with the jig and hold the pull up to check how it looks before you drill anything.

    Done right: the test marks look right with the pull held in place, and the jig settings are locked.

  3. Prevent tear-out

    Put painter's tape over the drilling spots on the front of the door. Hold or clamp a scrap block tight to the back of the door where the bit will come through. This stops the finish from chipping and the back from splintering.

    Done right: the tape is on the front and a backer block covers the exit point.

  4. Drill the holes

    Use the drill bit size listed with your hardware, often 3/16 in for standard 8-32 screws. Hold the drill square to the door and let the jig guide the bit. Drill all doors in one run, then all drawers, without changing jig settings in between.

    Done right: every hole is clean on the front, with no chipping when you peel off the tape.

  5. Attach the hardware

    Push the screws through from the back and thread them into the pull or knob. Tighten until snug. If the screws are too short for a thick door or drawer front, buy longer machine screws of the same thread.

    Done right: each pull is tight, level and lines up with its neighbors when you sight down the row.

Hire a pro if: you're filling old holes on painted or stained cabinets and want an invisible repair, or the cabinet doors are veneered and prone to chipping. A cabinet painter can fill, sand and refinish.

FAQ

Where should knobs go on cabinet doors?

On the stile opposite the hinges, about 2 to 3 in in from the corner: near the top on base cabinets and near the bottom on wall cabinets.

What size pulls should I use?

A common guideline is about one-third the width of the drawer. Standard sizes are 3 in, 96 mm and 128 mm center to center.

Can I reuse existing holes?

Yes, if the new hardware has the same center-to-center spacing. If not, you'll need to fill the old holes or use a backplate.

What drill bit size for cabinet handles?

Usually 3/16 in for standard 8-32 screws, but check your hardware's instructions.
